title: AP Psychology
summary: Practise research reasoning across the revised five-unit psychology framework.
frameworkNote: 2026–27 structure checked against College Board on 15 October 2026: 5 units. Original VertexED focused lessons and self-check questions sample each unit; they do not replace the full course framework, required materials or teacher review. Uses the revised five-unit framework, with research methods and data interpretation integrated throughout. Health scenarios are academic research exercises, not diagnoses or treatment advice.

modules.title: Biology and behaviour
modules.focus: Separate biological mechanisms from unwarranted causal claims.
explanation: Neurons transmit signals electrically along axons and chemically across many synapses. Neurotransmitters influence receiving cells through receptors; their effects depend on location and receptor type. Brain systems work in networks rather than as isolated boxes for single behaviours.

Biological findings need appropriate research methods. A correlation between brain activity and behaviour does not establish that the measured activity alone caused the behaviour. Operational definitions specify exactly how a variable was observed or measured.

workedExample.prompt: A study finds that students reporting less sleep also score lower on a memory task.
steps: Identify the association between measured sleep and memory scores.
Do not infer causation: stress or other variables may influence both.

misconception.claim: One neurotransmitter has one identical effect everywhere.
misconception.correction: Effects depend on receptors, pathways and interactions with other systems.

questions.prompt: Why should a sleep study define how sleep duration is measured?
questions.answer: A precise operational definition lets researchers interpret the variable and repeat the measurement consistently.

questions.prompt: Why does a brain-scan association not prove a region acts alone?
questions.answer: Multiple regions interact, and correlated activity does not isolate a unique or sufficient cause.

questions.hint: Explain how another researcher would repeat the measure.
questions.prompt: A study defines attention as the number of target symbols correctly marked in 60 seconds. What makes this operational, and name one limitation.
questions.answer: It states an observable scoring procedure and time window. It measures performance on this task, which can also depend on vision, motor speed or understanding and may not capture every aspect of attention.
hints: Explain how another researcher would repeat the measure.
Consider other processes that affect the same score.

questions.hint: Association can have more than one causal explanation.
questions.prompt: People who exercise more also perform better on a memory test in an observational sample. Why can the study not establish exercise as the cause?
questions.answer: Exercise was not randomly assigned, so differences such as sleep, health or prior habits could influence both exercise and memory, and directionality remains uncertain.
checkpoints: Explain the causal or directionality limitation.
hints: Association can have more than one causal explanation.
Look for factors related to both measured variables.

notes.title: Reasoning through biology and behaviour
paragraphs: Biological explanations connect behaviour with nervous-system processes, but a useful explanation must distinguish measurement from inference. A brain region can participate in a task without acting alone, and a correlation between neural activity and performance does not establish that the activity caused the performance. Operational definitions specify how a variable such as attention or sleep is recorded, allowing another researcher to repeat the procedure. Random assignment helps balance pre-existing differences between experimental groups; random sampling addresses which population the sample can represent. Neither procedure automatically removes measurement error, expectancy effects or the need for ethical safeguards.

workedExamples.prompt: A fictional experiment randomly assigns 40 volunteers to a quiet room or a room with recorded background speech, then measures recall of the same word list. Identify variables and one limit on generalisation.
steps: The manipulated independent variable is room sound condition; the dependent variable is number of words correctly recalled under a fixed scoring rule.
Random assignment strengthens a comparison between conditions, but volunteers from one setting may not represent every learner or real-world task.
workedExamples.conclusion: The design tests an effect of the sound condition on the defined recall outcome within a limited sample and task.

flashcards.back: A precise procedure for measuring or manipulating a variable.
Comparability of experimental groups.
Population representativeness when implemented appropriately.

flashcards.front: Does brain activation prove a region works alone?
flashcards.back: No; tasks involve interacting systems and measurement limitations.

modules.title: Memory, attention and thinking
explanation: Encoding, storage and retrieval are distinct memory processes. Attention affects what is encoded, while retrieval cues influence access. Working memory has limited capacity, so dividing attention can impair performance even when information seems familiar.

Memory is reconstructive: schemas and later information can alter recall. Retrieval practice and spaced review can support learning, but confidence and familiarity alone are poor evidence of accurate recall. A study must measure performance rather than infer it from feeling prepared.

workedExample.prompt: A learner recognises every term while rereading but cannot explain the terms with the book closed.
steps: Recognition supplies cues that free recall does not.
Use an unaided explanation to reveal retrieval gaps and guide the next review.

misconception.claim: A confident memory must be accurate.
misconception.correction: Confidence can be influenced by repetition and suggestion without improving accuracy.

questions.prompt: Why can a misleading question alter an eyewitness report?
questions.hint: Consider information introduced after the event.
questions.answer: The question may supply details that become incorporated into reconstructed memory.

questions.prompt: How does spacing differ from repeating a list ten times immediately?
questions.answer: Spacing distributes retrieval across time, requiring renewed access after some forgetting rather than immediate repetition.

questions.hint: Match the assessment to the skill.
questions.prompt: A learner rereads a definition and immediately recognises it, then cannot explain it tomorrow. Why is another recognition check alone weak evidence of independent recall?
questions.answer: Recognition supplies the target or strong cues, while independent recall requires generating the idea. A delayed explanation without the text more directly tests the missing skill.
checkpoints: Connect the test to the desired performance.
hints: Match the assessment to the skill.
Familiar appearance is not the same task as producing an explanation.

questions.hint: Consider how information from different occasions can be combined.
questions.prompt: After seeing a misleading description of an event, a witness includes that detail in a later account. Give a memory explanation without assuming deliberate lying.
questions.answer: Later information can be incorporated into reconstructive memory or confused with the original source, so a sincere report can include an inaccurate detail.
hints: Consider how information from different occasions can be combined.
An incorrect report need not be dishonest.

notes.title: Reasoning through memory, attention and thinking
paragraphs: Memory performance depends on encoding, retention and retrieval, so difficulty recalling an answer does not always mean no learning occurred. A recognition task supplies cues that can make an item feel familiar, while free recall requires generating it with fewer cues. Retrieval practice attempts to reconstruct an answer and then uses feedback to repair errors; merely viewing the answer first changes the task. Spacing distributes opportunities across time, requiring renewed retrieval after some forgetting. Memory is also reconstructive: later information and expectations can affect reports. Confidence and vividness are therefore evidence about a person’s experience, not guarantees of historical accuracy.

workedExamples.prompt: A learner gets 9 of 10 terms correct in a recognition quiz but only 4 of 10 in free recall. Design a next practice step and explain what the scores do not prove.
steps: Use a delayed closed-book recall attempt for the missed terms, then compare each answer with an accurate explanation and retry later.
The score difference shows cue dependence in these tasks; it does not prove that the learner has no knowledge or that recognition will always exceed recall by the same amount.
workedExamples.conclusion: Target retrieval with feedback while keeping the interpretation specific to the measured tasks.

flashcards.front: How does recognition differ from recall?
flashcards.back: Recognition identifies presented material; recall generates it with fewer supplied cues.

flashcards.front: Why attempt retrieval before viewing feedback?
flashcards.back: It reveals what can be produced independently.
Learning opportunities are separated across time.
No; memory reports can be confident yet mistaken.

modules.title: Development and learned behaviour
modules.focus: Distinguish classical conditioning from consequences of actions.
explanation: Development reflects interactions among biology, experience and context. Cross-sectional studies compare age groups at one time; longitudinal studies follow the same people over time. Cohort effects and participant attrition create different limitations.

Classical conditioning links stimuli, while operant conditioning changes behaviour through consequences. Reinforcement increases behaviour; punishment decreases it. Positive means adding a stimulus and negative means removing one, not good and bad.

workedExample.prompt: A seat-belt alarm stops when a driver buckles up, making buckling more frequent.
steps: An unpleasant stimulus is removed after the action.
Because the action increases, this is negative reinforcement.

misconception.claim: Negative reinforcement is another name for punishment.
misconception.correction: It removes a stimulus to increase behaviour; punishment decreases behaviour.

questions.prompt: A child receives praise after tidying and tidies more often. Classify the consequence.
questions.answer: Positive reinforcement: praise is added and tidying increases.

questions.prompt: Why might a cross-sectional age comparison confuse age with cohort?
questions.answer: Different age groups grew up under different conditions, so observed differences may reflect cohort experiences rather than ageing alone.

questions.prompt: A fictional game removes points after a rule violation, and violations become less frequent. Classify the consequence using both dimensions.
questions.answer: It is negative punishment: something valued is removed and the target behaviour decreases.
hints: Track points and behaviour separately.
Use observed frequency rather than whether the consequence seems unpleasant.

questions.hint: The groups did not grow up in the same conditions.
questions.prompt: A study compares today’s 20-year-olds with today’s 70-year-olds on technology use. Why is the difference not automatically a developmental effect of ageing?
questions.answer: The groups experienced different educational, cultural and technological histories. These cohort differences can affect technology use independently of within-person ageing.
checkpoints: Distinguish between-group differences from within-person change.
hints: The groups did not grow up in the same conditions.
Ask what a longitudinal comparison would add.

notes.title: Reasoning through development and learned behaviour
paragraphs: Learning theories classify how experience changes behaviour, but their terms must be applied to observable effects. Reinforcement increases a behaviour’s future frequency; punishment decreases it. Positive means adding a consequence and negative means removing one, not beneficial versus harmful. Classical conditioning concerns learned associations between stimuli, whereas operant conditioning concerns relations between behaviour and consequences. Developmental research additionally distinguishes change within individuals from differences between age groups. A longitudinal design follows the same participants and can reveal trajectories, but attrition and repeated testing can bias results; a cross-sectional design is faster but can confound age with cohort experience.

workedExamples.prompt: A classroom removes a disliked extra chore when students submit work on time, and on-time submissions subsequently increase. Classify the process.
steps: The consequence removes an aversive condition, so it is negative in the technical add/remove sense.
The target behaviour increases, so the consequence functions as reinforcement rather than punishment.
workedExamples.conclusion: This is negative reinforcement of on-time submission in the stated observations.

flashcards.back: An increase in the future frequency of a behaviour.

flashcards.front: What does negative mean in conditioning terminology?
flashcards.back: A consequence is removed.
It decreases the behaviour’s future frequency.
Age groups differ in shared historical experiences as well as age.

modules.title: Social influence and personality
modules.focus: Explain behaviour through both situations and dispositions.
explanation: Attribution concerns explanations for behaviour. People may overemphasise personal traits while underestimating situational constraints when judging others. Social norms, roles and group expectations can influence choices even when individuals hold different private views.

Personality measures describe patterns but require reliability and validity. A consistent questionnaire is not necessarily measuring the intended trait. Research involving social influence must consider informed consent, justified deception, debriefing and participants’ welfare.

workedExample.prompt: A student arrives late and is labelled careless, although the bus broke down.
steps: The label attributes behaviour to a stable personal quality.
The transport failure provides a situational explanation that the judgement ignored.

misconception.claim: A reliable test is automatically valid.
misconception.correction: Consistent scores do not prove that a test measures its intended construct.

questions.prompt: How can normative social influence produce conformity?
questions.answer: People may match group behaviour to gain approval or avoid rejection even when privately disagreeing.

questions.prompt: A scale gives identical but wrong weights. Which measurement distinction does it illustrate?
questions.answer: It illustrates reliability without validity for accurate weight measurement.

questions.hint: Measure belief separately from visible agreement.
questions.prompt: A student gives an incorrect group answer publicly but the correct answer privately. What distinction does this illustrate?
questions.answer: Public conformity can differ from private belief; the public answer alone does not demonstrate internal acceptance of the group’s view.
checkpoints: Limit the inference from the public behaviour.
hints: Measure belief separately from visible agreement.
Do not infer a motive beyond the evidence unless supplied.

questions.hint: Consistency and measuring the right thing are different criteria.
questions.prompt: A personality scale gives similar scores each week but mostly measures reading difficulty rather than the intended trait. Evaluate reliability and validity.
questions.answer: The repeated consistency supports test-retest reliability in this sample, but measuring reading difficulty undermines construct validity for the intended trait.
hints: Consistency and measuring the right thing are different criteria.
Keep the claim limited to the evidence supplied.

notes.title: Reasoning through social influence and personality
paragraphs: Social explanations examine how situations, group norms and interpretations affect behaviour without assuming everyone responds identically. Attribution distinguishes explanations based on a person’s dispositions from those based on circumstances. A single observation usually cannot separate them, so compare behaviour across settings and occasions. Normative influence can lead someone to agree publicly to gain acceptance even when private beliefs differ, while informational influence involves treating others as evidence about reality. Personality measures require both reliability and validity: consistent scores do not establish that the instrument measures the intended construct or predicts the relevant behaviour across populations.

workedExamples.prompt: In a group task, a participant privately selects answer B but publicly agrees with a unanimous group choosing A to avoid disapproval. Identify the influence and a useful follow-up measure.
steps: The stated motive indicates normative influence: public agreement serves social acceptance rather than necessarily changing private belief.
Collect a confidential answer after the group session to examine whether private belief also changed, without assuming the public response proves it.
workedExamples.conclusion: The example supports normative influence and calls for a separate measure of private belief.

flashcards.back: An explanation based on a person’s characteristics.
An explanation based on circumstances.
Acceptance or avoidance of social disapproval.
No; a measure can consistently assess the wrong construct.

modules.title: Stress, health and evidence
modules.focus: Evaluate psychological claims without diagnosing from a brief description.
explanation: Stress involves appraisal of demands and available coping resources. Physiological responses can be useful in the short term, while prolonged stress can affect health. Social support and context influence how people experience and respond to stressors.

Psychological disorders involve patterns assessed within clinical, cultural and developmental contexts. A single behaviour or classroom vignette is insufficient for diagnosis. Treatment evidence should consider controls, outcome measures, sample characteristics and possible confounding variables.

workedExample.prompt: A fictional study reports lower stress after a programme, but includes no comparison group.
steps: The observed change is consistent with improvement.
Time, expectations or other changes could explain it; the programme’s causal effect remains uncertain.

misconception.claim: One unusual behaviour identifies a mental disorder.
misconception.correction: Assessment requires a broader pattern, context and qualified evaluation.

questions.prompt: Why might random assignment improve a treatment study?
questions.answer: It helps balance participant characteristics across groups, strengthening causal comparisons when implemented properly.

questions.prompt: Why report both average improvement and variation across participants?
questions.answer: A mean can hide people who improve little or worsen; variation shows how consistent the outcomes are.

questions.prompt: A programme group improves by 8 points while its comparison improves by 5. Find the difference in change and explain why the programme’s full eight-point change is not the comparison-based effect estimate.
questions.answer: The difference is 3 points. The comparison also improved, so some change may reflect factors shared by both groups rather than the programme alone.
checkpoints: Recognise improvement in the comparison group.
Explain why before-after change alone overattributes shared change.
hints: Subtract the comparison’s change.
A programme group is not its own complete counterfactual.

questions.hint: A single average hides a distribution.
questions.prompt: A report gives a mean improvement of 4 points but no spread or follow-up. Name two questions that remain and explain their relevance.
questions.answer: How variable were individual changes, and did improvement persist? Spread informs consistency and possible adverse or null outcomes; follow-up informs durability.
checkpoints: Connect each missing detail to interpretation of the mean.
hints: A single average hides a distribution.
Immediate and sustained effects are different outcomes.

notes.title: Reasoning through stress, health and evidence
paragraphs: Health and stress research needs careful comparisons because outcomes can change over time for many reasons. A before-after improvement may reflect the programme, natural fluctuation, expectations, concurrent events or regression towards typical values after an unusually difficult period. Random assignment to an appropriate comparison group helps address some alternative explanations, while ethical consent, privacy and participant welfare remain necessary. Report distributions and effect sizes alongside averages so readers can see variation and practical magnitude. A group-level association or intervention result does not by itself diagnose an individual or identify a universally effective response for every person.

workedExamples.prompt: A fictional stress programme has mean scores 20 before and 14 after. A randomised comparison group changes from 19 to 15. Compare the changes and state a limit.
steps: The programme group improves by 6 points and the comparison by 4, giving a difference in change of 2 points.
Without sample sizes, variability, measurement quality and follow-up, this difference alone cannot establish precision, durability or individual benefit.
workedExamples.conclusion: The observed extra improvement is 2 points, with important uncertainty still unmeasured.

flashcards.back: To assess changes that could occur without the intervention.

flashcards.front: What is regression towards the mean?
flashcards.back: Extreme measured scores often become less extreme on repeat measurement partly through random variation.

flashcards.front: Why report variation as well as a mean?
flashcards.back: Participants can have very different outcomes.

flashcards.front: Does a group mean diagnose an individual?
flashcards.back: No.
